source.title: Watch the Weights: Unsupervised monitoring and control of fine-tuned LLMs

record.tranche_reason: Tests recovery after unlearning using weight-derived activation steering, a different internal intervention from the claim's cited examples.
record.gate_note: The unlearning detection rates in Table 4 show that inputs about unlearned topics can be flagged, but do not by themselves measure knowledge recovery, so they are not rows. Results cited from prior work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study removes weight-derived activation directions at inference time (orthogonalizing activations against them) in published unlearned models. It reports how much forgotten knowledge or harmful compliance comes back: WMDP accuracy for Zephyr-RMU, HarmBench ASR for Circuit Breaker, and a qualitative example for WHP. This is a different method aimed at version C's question of whether a direction ablation restores unlearned content, and the results also bear on A's robustness claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say weight-derived steering 'can sometimes' recover unlearned capabilities. They recover 77% of Zephyr-RMU's lost WMDP-Bio accuracy and 39% of Cyber, which they say matches the supervised result of Arditi & Chughtai and confirms RMU unlearning is shallow. With a prefill, steering takes Circuit Breaker's HarmBench ASR to 82.08%. They attribute WHP's resistance to deeper 'belief-level' edits from SFT-based unlearning.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weight-difference singular vectors to steer activations at inference time; it does not fine-tune on recovery data, ablate a tested direction, or quantize weights.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varies by unlearning method: WHP is resistant while Zephyr-RMU and Circuit Breaker show recovery. Zephyr-RMU recovery is greater with calibration ranges trimmed by 0.1% at each end, alongside a rise in FPR from 0.94% to 8.54%.

fits_no_version.finding: With low FPR, WeightWatch flags 34 to 95% of queries or completions on unlearned topics (Table 4). The open-ended audit finds unlearned content among extremal transcripts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearned models retain detectable topic-specific activation signatures along fine-tuning weight directions.

record.problems: The Zephyr-RMU recovery results involve increased false positives at the more aggressive setting. The Circuit Breaker result combines steering with a prompt prefix, so the contribution of each is not isolated. The WHP steering evidence is qualitative, and no uncertainty estimates are reported for the recovery results.

untested.parts: Only weight-derived steering attacks are tested. There is no relearning, quantization or prompting-only attack. No new unlearning method is assessed.
No analysis, beyond steering, of whether knowledge is blocked rather than deleted (e.g., probing for retained representations).
No prompting-only recovery of knowledge. Prefilling alone on Circuit Breaker is reported only as a jailbreak baseline.
No robust unlearning method is proposed or tested.

missing.what: Circuit Breaker ASR under prefilling alone (0.0%), RepE (0.0%) and input embedding (9.6%). Steered vs unsteered MMLU, GSM8K and HellaSwag (58.9/64.8/63.9 vs 58.8/64.4/64.4).
Zephyr-RMU before vs after unlearning: WMDP-Bio 63.7 to 31.2 and Cyber 44.0 to 28.2 (near chance); MMLU 58.1 to 57.1. These show the A-type baseline the study measured.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche T2: activation-direction ablation found without supervision, applied to published unlearned models. The record's claim that steering and prefix are not isolated is overstated, because prefilling alone yields 0.0% ASR. The main recovery figure for Zephyr-RMU requires loosening the calibration (FPR 8.54%). No uncertainty is reported. The WHP evidence is a single example.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish a near-chance reference for targeted knowledge or test whether general ability is preserved across unlearning methods. Tests steering recovery for Zephyr-RMU and a refusal-bypass attack for Circuit Breaker, not the full range of simple attacks.
No fine-tuning or relearning on a small set of examples.

Uses activation steering by projecting activations against weight-derived directions, not a direct ablation test. Does not directly establish that retained information is stored in the weights rather than inferable through another mechanism.
No prompting-only, rephrasing, language, or in-context recovery test. The Circuit Breaker attack combines steering with a prompt prefix, so it does not isolate prompting.
WeightWatch is presented as a monitoring and steering approach, not as a method tested for resistance to the attacks in the claim.

rows.subject: WHP
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned on obfuscated Harry Potter facts
rows.operation_detail: Applied activation steering along identified directions to questions about unlearned Harry Potter content.
rows.baseline: Unsteered response included incorrect Harry Potter-related beliefs.
rows.value: Steering partially restored Harry Potter references, but incorrect beliefs remained.
rows.note: The example still gives the wrong author and fictional details after steering.
rows.check: It is a single qualitative example, and the authors label it 'failed steering' and call WHP 'quite resistant'. The Harry Potter name returns, but the wrong author and invented facts remain, so recovery is at most minimal.

rows.subject: Circuit Breaker
rows.stage_stated: unlearned harmful content with representation rerouting
rows.operation_detail: Combined directional activation steering with the prompt prefix “Sure, I can help with that! Here is a detailed guide:”.
rows.note: This is a combined steering-and-prefix result; it does not isolate a prompting-only effect.
rows.check: The 9.6% baseline is the ASR of an input-embedding attack, not of the unattacked model. In Table 11, prefilling alone and RepE both give 0.0%, so the steering's contribution is largely isolated, contrary to the record's note. ASR measures harmful compliance judged by GPT-4o-mini, not knowledge accuracy. The operation is activation ablation plus a prefill, not a weight edit.

source_check.correct: Table 11: 9.6% is the Input Embed attack ASR on the After Unlearning model. Prefilling alone gives 0.0% and RepE 0.0%; Prefilling (w/ Steering, FPR 0.90%) gives 82.08%. The authors' summary does say 'from 9.6% to 82.08%'. The baseline should name the input-embed attack, or use the 0.0% prefilling-alone value.
source_check.problem: The 9.6% baseline is the input-embedding attack's ASR, not the unattacked unlearned model's.

source_check.notes: Every row's op says weight_edit, but the method orthogonalizes activations at inference (directional ablation), so it fits C's 'ablating a direction'. The r12 baseline of 9.6% is the input-embed attack. The 82.08% needs prefill plus steering. The authors call the RMU recovery 'partial' overall, so r1's observed state (77% of the loss) is borderline.

statements.correction: 2508.00161 method: when flagged, projects activations off the top singular vectors of the O_proj/W_down weight differences (directional ablation at inference, Sec 3). Zephyr-RMU WMDP-Bio 31.2 to 56.2 of 63.7 at 8.54% FPR, MMLU 57.1 to 57.0. Circuit Breaker ASR 82.08% with steering plus prefill, 0.0% prefill alone.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the method is misread. The study does not add a vector. When a token is flagged, it orthogonalizes activations against weight-difference singular vectors, a − (a·u)u. That is directional ablation, yet the conditions say 'activation addition/subtraction (not ablation)'.

statements.correction: 8.54% FPR: Cyber 28.2 to 34.3 (38.6% of the loss), Bio 77%. 0.94% FPR: Bio 31.2 to 39.7 (about 26%), Cyber 28.2 to 31.4 (about 20%).
statements.problem: '(20–39% of the loss)' comes right after the 0.94% FPR values, but 39% is the Cyber figure at 8.54% FPR. At 0.94% the range is 20–26%.

statements.problem: The WHP result and its limits_scope label are right. But the conditions call the attacks 'activation-addition', and this study's steering removes the component along weight-derived directions (directional ablation).
